title: Payment Reliability at Scale: What Enterprise Businesses Need Across Southeast Asia
summary: Payment reliability at scale determines how much demand becomes revenue. See what enterprise businesses need from payment infrastructure across Southeast Asia. The post Payment Reliability at Scale: What Enterprise Businesses Need Across Southeast Asia appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Payment reliability becomes harder to hold onto as your transaction volumes grow.


**Southeast Asia's gross transaction value** for


**digital payments** was expected to


[exceed US$1 trillion in 2025](https://www.mastercard.com/news/ap/en/perspectives/en/2024/tech-trends-and-trust-making-south-east-asia-s-digital-economy-work-for-all/) , and that value moves through digital payment methods including e-wallets, QR payments, bank transfers, and cards. For enterprise businesses, payment reliability at scale therefore decides how much of that demand your business actually collects.


When digital payments carry that much commercial value, an outage interrupts a primary payment method instead of a minor backup option, which raises what every minute of disruption costs your business.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- What payment reliability includes at enterprise scale, from availability through payment event delivery


- Why more transactions and more payment rails increase what your infrastructure has to get right


- The criteria to apply when you evaluate payment infrastructure for a multi-market operation


- How Xendit maintains 99.999% uptime, handles delayed events, and exposes payment status your teams can act on


- How tiket.com processes transaction surges of up to 17x without dropping payment success rates


## **What a payment disruption costs enterprise businesses in Southeast Asia**


Payment activity across Southeast Asia is


**fragmented** , with each market developing its own payment methods and consumer habits.


In


**Indonesia** ,


[QRIS](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/qris) has become a


**central part of the local payment** ecosystem.


[Indonesian fintech and e-commerce companies](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2026/042/article-A002-en.xml) have integrated QRIS into their applications so customers can pay through a single national QR standard. If you sell in Indonesia, the availability of that one payment method affects a meaningful share of your checkout attempts.


In


**the Philippines** ,


[e-wallets](https://www.xendit.co/en-ph/blog/e-wallets-in-the-philippines-a-business-guide-to-accepting-gcash-maya-and-more/) carry most of the transaction activity.


[Payment data from the travel industry in 2025](https://www.xendit.co/en/xendit-2025-travel-payments-report/) showed that e-wallets accounted for


**66.4%** of payment transactions in the market. An e-wallet disruption in the Philippines therefore hits your sales harder than a card disruption would.


In


**Thailand** , adoption has grown through bank-based payments.


[PromptPay](https://www.xendit.co/en-th/blog/accepting-mobile-banking-payments-in-thailand-a-complete-guide-for-businesses/) transactions


[grew more than eightfold between 2019 and 2024](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2026/042/article-A002-en.xml) , while e-money adoption in Thailand is high compared with regional peers. Thai customers use PromptPay often enough that they expect it to work at your checkout the same way it works everywhere else they pay.


Fragmentation also changes what happens at the moment a customer is ready to pay, because a problem with one payment method can end a transaction the customer had already committed to. Visa found that


[6 in 10 consumers in Asia Pacific](https://www.visa.com.sg/about-visa/stories/2025/commerce-of-tomorrow-why-ecommerce-growth-in-asia-pacific-depends-on-frictionless-secure-payments.html) had experienced


**card issues** in the previous year, and


**47%** said they would either


**visit another merchant or abandon the purchase** after encountering card issues at checkout. Close to half of the customers who meet a payment problem at your checkout therefore do not stay to try again.


That behavior gets expensive at


**enterprise volume** . A regional retailer processing a million payment attempts a month, an online travel platform confirming tens of thousands of bookings a day, and a SaaS company running renewals across six markets are all collecting from thousands of customers in any given minute. A few minutes of disruption can therefore affect thousands of transactions at once.


**Peak periods** raise the stakes further. Campaign days, flash sales, and ticket releases concentrate


**a large share of monthly demand into a few hours** , so a short disruption inside one of those windows reaches far more customers than the same disruption on an ordinary day.


***Also read:***[Enterprise Payment Infrastructure for Peak E-Commerce Traffic: A Southeast Asia Guide](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/enterprise-payment-infrastructure-for-peak-e-commerce-traffic-a-southeast-asia-guide/)


**Payment reliability at enterprise scale** therefore describes three things working together. Your infrastructure


**stays available** when customers transact,


**recovers from disruption** without manual intervention, and


**moves payment events accurately** into the systems that act on them. Keeping an API online covers only the first. Your business should care about all three because each one maps to revenue captured at the point of intent and to operational work your engineering and finance teams either avoid or absorb afterward.


## **What payment reliability means at enterprise scale**


Most payment providers describe reliability with a single uptime percentage. That figure tells you whether the system was running, and it leaves out two things that decide your revenue, which are whether customers finished paying and whether your own systems received the result.


Here are


**three conditions that determine whether a payment completes and reaches your systems correctly** at enterprise scale:


### **1. Availability when customers are ready to pay**


Payment uptime works differently from uptime for a conventional software product. SaaS uptime is usually calculated at overall system or feature level, while in payments the measure that counts commercially is whether an end user can complete a payment at the intended time without failure or delay. Xendit compares that requirement to critical utilities such as electricity, which have to be available continuously.


***Also read:***[What Defines Payment Reliability and How Do We Measure It? How Xendit Ensures 99.999% Uptime](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/xendit-payment-reliability-99-999-uptime/)


For your business, a payment platform reporting healthy system availability while payment attempts fail at checkout delivers none of the outcome you are paying for. A short disruption converts into failed transactions, customer drop-off, and revenue you already spent on the acquisition budget to earn.


### **2. Accurate payment status and event delivery**


A completed customer payment has to become an accurate payment status inside your own systems. Xendit


[sends that status to you as a webhook](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/handling-webhooks) , which is an automated message confirming what happened to a payment, and your systems use it to trigger order fulfillment, reconciliation, and customer notifications. Local payment methods in this region can take hours or days to process, so the confirmation rarely arrives at the same moment the customer finishes paying.


When status updates arrive late or never arrive, your operations team carries discrepancies even though the customer already paid. The order stays unfulfilled, support answers a question it cannot verify, and finance takes an unexplained line into reconciliation.


### **3. Recovery when something goes wrong**


Your engineering team should assume that individual components, connections, and partner systems will fail at some point. The question worth putting to a payment provider is how quickly their system detects a failure, recovers, and continues processing. Xendit builds redundancy, monitoring, controlled releases, and failover into how we


[maintain payment reliability](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/xendit-payment-reliability-99-999-uptime/) .


That distinction decides whether an incident becomes a brief dip in one metric or a manual recovery exercise your teams spend the following week resolving.


Availability, accurate event delivery, and recovery apply at any transaction volume. What changes as your business grows is how much work each one has to do.


## **Why payment reliability gets harder as your payment operations scale**


Growth adds transactions, payment methods, markets, and downstream systems at the same time, and every addition gives your payment infrastructure more to keep working correctly.


Here are


**three effects that put the most pressure on payment reliability as your operations grow** across Southeast Asia:


###


**1. More payment methods create more dependencies**


Serving customers across Southeast Asia can mean supporting cards, e-wallets, QR payments, bank transfers, and other local methods, since alternative payment methods from digital wallets to QR codes have reshaped how the region pays (Mastercard, 2025). Each of the


[payment channels](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) you activate carries its own processing flow, partner connections, and points of failure.


Your reliability requirement therefore covers the wider payment ecosystem instead of a single payment API. A provider that performs well on cards and poorly on the e-wallet your Philippine customers use daily leaves your business exposed in the market where it can least afford to be.


### **2. Small reliability gaps become material at high volume**


Percentages that look minor in a monthly report describe real customers once transaction counts grow. Take a business handling one million payment attempts in a month. A 0.5% rate of affected transactions works out to 5,000 payment attempts that did not complete as intended.


That figure is worth modeling against your own volume before you sign a provider, because 5,000 affected attempts in a month means a comparable number repeating every month until the underlying cause changes.


### **3. Reliability extends past the initial payment attempt**


A payment moves through several stages before your business can treat it as complete, and each stage can fail independently of the others. The full journey covers:


- Payment initiation


- Authentication


- Payment confirmation


- Webhook and event delivery


- Order fulfillment


- Settlement and reconciliation


A reliable payment operation therefore needs visibility across all six stages. Delayed or failed callbacks from banks can create missing transactions,[which automated reconciliation](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/settlements-overview) then identifies and processes, sometimes only after one or several days during a bank system outage. Your finance team should build that possibility into your[reconciliation process](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) , so a delayed callback becomes a known exception instead of an unexplained gap at month-end. Knowing where reliability breaks down gives you the criteria to assess it in a provider.

## **What to look for in enterprise payment infrastructure across Southeast Asia**


Payment providers describe their own reliability in different terms, which makes a direct comparison difficult. Turning those claims into specific questions gives your team one consistent basis for evaluating each provider.


Here are


**five areas to cover when you evaluate enterprise payment infrastructure** for Southeast Asia:


- **Consistent availability** Can your customers complete payments whenever they are ready to transact, including outside business hours and during campaign peaks? Ask your payment provider for a documented uptime record that reports API traffic and webhook traffic separately, since one platform-wide figure can average out a weakness in either one. Ask how that uptime is measured and over what period, so your team compares the same thing across providers.


- **Resilience and recovery** What happens when a dependent system, network, or partner service fails temporarily? Ask whether retries, redundancy, and failover run automatically without your team raising a ticket, how quickly incidents are usually detected and resolved, and whether your engineers can test failure scenarios in a sandbox environment before you go live.


- **Payment visibility** Can your technical and operations teams identify payment status and issues without assembling information from several systems? Ask which status fields and failure reasons are exposed through the dashboard, the API, and downloadable reports. Your teams should be able to separate a failed payment from a delayed status update and from a downstream processing issue, because each one calls for a different response.


- **Broad payment coverage** Does your payment infrastructure support the payment methods your customers use in every market you serve, and can you


[add a method](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) without rebuilding your payment architecture? An available platform that lacks the local payment options your customers prefer may cost you the transaction, so coverage and reliability have to be assessed together.


- **Scalability** Can the same payment infrastructure absorb higher transaction volumes, additional payment methods, and new markets without a matching increase in operational complexity for your team? Ask what API rate limits apply per endpoint and per account, and how much advance notice they need to raise those limits. Those two answers tell your engineering team whether a campaign peak will be capped by the platform before anything else.


Applying these five criteria to a specific provider is where the detail matters, so here is how Xendit approaches each one.


## **How Xendit supports payment reliability for enterprise businesses in Southeast Asia**


Xendit treats payment reliability as an engineering


**standard** across uptime, infrastructure design, release process, incident response, event delivery, and reporting. Here is how each part of that works for an enterprise payment operation:


### **1. 99.999% uptime across APIs and webhooks**


Since 2025,


**Xendit has maintained**[99.999% uptime](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/xendit-payment-reliability-99-999-uptime/) **for overall traffic across its APIs and webhooks** , meaning only 0.001% of traffic was ever affected by downtime. Each additional nine in an uptime figure reduces the downtime allowed in a year by an order of magnitude:


- 99.9% uptime (three nines) allows approximately 43 minutes of downtime per month, equivalent to 8.6 hours per year


- 99.99% uptime (four nines) reduces that to around 4 minutes per month, equivalent to 48 minutes per year


- 99.999% uptime (five nines) reduces it further to approximately 5 minutes and 15 seconds per year


**Xendit operates at that third level** . For an enterprise business, the practical difference is large. At one million payment attempts a month, the gap between 8.6 hours and


**roughly 5 minutes of annual downtime** separates thousands of customers meeting a failed checkout from almost none.


### **2. Backup systems that keep payments running during a failure**


Xendit builds redundancy across critical infrastructure so a single failure does not take down the broader payment system, including a multi-availability zone setup where services run across three separate data centers in case one fails partially or completely.


For your business, that design decides what a cloud provider incident means in practice. Losing one data center becomes a routing decision inside the payment platform instead of an outage your customers experience at checkout.


### **3. Monitoring, release discipline, and incident response**


Xendit maintains full monitoring and alerting coverage across our systems, with dashboards giving real-time visibility into traffic at a granular level so errors can be traced to a root cause and remediated quickly. Your own teams get a matching view of live payment activity in the


[Xendit Dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/your-dashboard) , so both sides work from current data during an incident.


Releases move through testing and approvals in environments that mimic production, followed by controlled canary rollout with continuous monitoring, rollback when error rates or anomalies appear, and off-peak scheduling for large or critical changes. Your engineers can also


[simulate success, error, and failure scenarios](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/simulate-error-scenarios) with a Test Mode API key, so your own error handling is tested before it meets live traffic.


When an anomaly is detected, either through monitoring or from a customer or partner report, the firewarden on shift, meaning the engineer on duty for incident response, is alerted along with senior engineering managers and CTO office members. A working group forms within minutes to identify the root cause and apply mitigation.


For your business, that protocol shows up as shorter detection and resolution times, which keeps an incident from becoming a backlog of failed transactions your team has to unpick afterward.


Reliability of this kind comes from how the infrastructure is operated day to day, which is difficult to retrofit once an incident has already happened.


### **4. Automatic retries and handling for delayed events**


Payment events reaching your systems form the second half of a completed payment. Xendit


[automatically re-delivers unsuccessful webhooks](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/webhook-behavior) up to six times until it receives a 2XX response from your server, with exponential backoff at 15 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours, 6 hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours from the original attempt. Your team can also resend specific events from the Webhook tab in the dashboard, or use custom retry to resend a filtered batch of up to 500 webhooks at once after a longer interruption on your side.


Some payment confirmations arrive late for reasons outside the retry mechanism, including a provider confirming a payment after a delay, or Xendit detecting a payment during reconciliation that the provider never reported. Xendit documents each of those


[delayed webhook scenarios](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/delayed-webhooks) with recommended handling, including holding an order for up to 24 hours, the average Xendit reconciliation time, when the customer can produce a payment receipt. Deciding that policy in advance turns a late confirmation into a documented process for your operations team instead of a support ticket handled case by case.


### **5. Payment status your teams can act on**


Xendit reports


[transaction status and settlement status](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transaction-status) as a pair across the dashboard, API responses, and reports, so a payment captured and awaiting settlement reads differently from one voided before any ledger posting or reversed after settlement. Your teams can separate a payment problem from a settlement timing question without raising a ticket to find out which one they have.


For investigation, the


[transactions report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) carries status, channel, fees, settlement status, settlement date, and your own reference on a single line per transaction, with a


[detailed version](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/detailed-transactions-report) available for deeper analysis. Reports can be exported on demand or


[scheduled](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/scheduling-reports) to email or SFTP, so your finance team works from the same record your engineering team uses.


### **6. Rate limits and capacity planning before peak volume**


Enterprise traffic runs into platform limits before it runs into anything else, so those limits belong in your capacity planning. Xendit applies


[API rate limiting](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/rate-limits) per endpoint per account, set at 600 requests per minute in Live mode, with response headers reporting your remaining quota and the time left in the current window. Requests above that limit receive a 429 response, which your system should handle by throttling and retrying instead of treating the payment as failed.


Businesses expecting sustained higher throughput can request an increase, which Xendit asks to receive at least four weeks in advance. Raising it while you plan a campaign costs your team nothing, and raising it during one is usually too late.


### **7. Regional payment infrastructure**


Xendit provides access to


[multiple payment methods](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) through a single integration and supports payment operations across its Southeast Asian markets,


[under licensed entities in each one](https://www.xendit.co/en/company/xendit-licenses/) . Reliability confined to one market or one payment method leaves an enterprise operating regionally exposed everywhere else, so the same availability, recovery, and event delivery standards need to extend across every payment method your customers use.


## **How tiket.com holds performance during ticket wars, processing 17x transaction surges without dropping payments**


[tiket.com](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/tiket/) is one of Indonesia's leading online travel agents, selling flights and hotels alongside tickets to major events. Two payment problems came with that model:


1. Indonesia has


**dozens of ways for customers to pay** , and covering enough of them would normally mean managing several payment providers at once.


2. Ticket sales for high-demand events create


**ticket wars** , where the


**average transaction rate can surge by up to 17x** its normal level within minutes.


Through a single integration with Xendit, tiket.com accepts credit and debit card payments alongside


**a wider**[range of local payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , with 3DS 2.0 allowing customers to bypass OTP at checkout. During those 17x surges, the platform maintained its usual


**transaction processing on 99.99% API uptime** from Xendit, with payment success rates holding and card validation and fraud detection keeping transactions secure.


This shows where enterprise reliability is genuinely tested. Processing transactions at normal volume is the baseline every provider clears, and holding performance when demand multiplies within minutes is the standard your infrastructure has to meet.


## **Keep your payment operations dependable as transaction volumes grow**


Payment reliability determines how much of the demand you already paid to create turns into completed transactions. At enterprise scale, it covers availability, resilience when a dependency fails, accurate payment event delivery, visibility across the payment journey, and the ability to operate across multiple payment methods and markets.


For businesses operating across Southeast Asia, choosing payment infrastructure with those capabilities reduces disruption and keeps payment operations dependable as volume grows. Xendit's 99.999% API and webhook uptime, infrastructure redundancy, monitoring and release discipline, automatic recovery mechanisms, transaction-level reporting, and regional payment coverage are built to support that reliability at the volumes enterprise businesses run.

## **FAQ for enterprise businesses in Southeast Asia: Payment reliability at scale**


### **What uptime should an enterprise business expect from a payment provider in Southeast Asia?**


Ask for uptime that covers API and webhook traffic together, since a platform can stay available while payment events fail to reach your systems.


**Xendit** has


[maintained 99.999% uptime](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/xendit-payment-reliability-99-999-uptime/) across its overall API and webhook traffic since 2025, which works out to approximately 5 minutes and 15 seconds of downtime per year. At enterprise volume, that figure decides how many transactions clear during your busiest trading periods.


### **What happens to payment notifications if our system is down when a payment completes?**


**Xendit**[re-delivers unsuccessful webhooks](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/webhook-behavior) up to six times with exponential backoff, spread across 24 hours from the original attempt, until it receives a 2XX response from your server. Your team can also resend individual events from the Webhook tab in the


[Xendit Dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/your-dashboard) , or resend a filtered batch of up to 500 webhooks at once after a longer outage. Your business recovers the payment events without rebuilding transaction records by hand.


### **How do you prevent duplicate processing when webhooks are retried or arrive out of order?**


Retries and provider-side recovery can produce duplicate webhooks for the same event, and network or processing delays can deliver events in a jumbled sequence.


**Xendit** provides unique server-side IDs, including payment_id and capture_id, so your system can


[validate each event](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/handling-webhooks) before releasing goods or services, signs each event with a token in the x-callback-token header for authentication, and recommends a messaging queue as a buffer so your system picks events up once all of them have arrived. Those practices protect your business against duplicate fulfillment and the money loss that follows it.


### **What should we do when a payment confirmation arrives hours after the customer paid?**


Late confirmations usually come from a payment method provider reporting a payment after a delay, or from Xendit detecting the payment during reconciliation when the provider never reported it. Xendit's guidance on


[delayed webhooks](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/delayed-webhooks) recommends asking the customer for their payment receipt and holding the order up to 24 hours, the average Xendit


[reconciliation](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) time, or terminating the order and refunding once


[settlement](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/settlements-overview) arrives. Agreeing that policy in advance gives your operations team a consistent response instead of a judgment call each time.


### **How do we tell a failed payment apart from a delayed status update?**


**Xendit** exposes


[transaction status and settlement status](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transaction-status) as a pair in the dashboard, API responses, and reports, so a successful payment awaiting settlement is distinguishable from one that was voided, failed, or reversed after settlement. Your teams read both fields to decide whether an issue belongs to the payment itself or to settlement timing. The transactions report carries the same fields per transaction, so finance and engineering work from one record.


### **Are there API rate limits we should plan for at high transaction volume?**


Yes, and they belong in your capacity planning before a campaign rather than during one.


**Xendit** sets


[API rate limits](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/rate-limits) per endpoint per account at 600 requests per minute in Live mode, returns your remaining quota in the response headers, and responds with a 429 and RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED when the limit is passed. Businesses expecting sustained higher throughput can request an increase, and Xendit asks for that request at least four weeks ahead.


### **Why do transactions go missing at settlement, and how are they recovered?**


Missing transactions usually trace back to


[delayed or failed callbacks](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/settlements-overview) from banks, caused by temporary connectivity issues, bank-side processing delays, or network interruptions during the callback.


**Xendit** runs automated reconciliation to identify and process these transactions, and during bank system downtime its reconciliation system may only be informed about them after one or several days. Your finance team should keep flexibility in its


[reconciliation process](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) for those cases, and can contact Xendit support with the reference ID, amount, and date to resolve a specific transaction.
